claim: The study includes 12 recording sessions from three macaque monkeys (M: 3, S: 6 and Z: 3).
source: The current study includes 12 recording sessions from three macaque monkeys (M: 3, S: 6 and Z: 3).
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text with specific numbers of sessions per monkey.

claim: Recordings were obtained from the ventral premotor (F5), anterior intraparietal (AIP), and primary motor (M1) cortex areas.
source: We recorded from the grasping motor network, including part of the ventral premotor (F5), anterior intraparietal (AIP), and additionally from primary motor (M1) cortex area for monkey M (Schaffelhofer and Scherberger, 2016) (Table 1).
evidence: Directly stated in the text with citation support for the recording locations.

claim: An average of 570 trials (SD: 177) were recorded in each session.
source: An average number of 570 trials (SD: 177) were recorded in each session.
evidence: Directly stated with specific numerical data including standard deviation.

claim: An average of 88 single units (SD: 32) were recorded in parallel.
source: In each area, recordings were obtained from two floating microelectrode arrays (FMAs), for a total of 64 channels (32 per microarray) per area (Figure 1B; see Materials and methods) from which an average of 88 single units (SD: 32) were recorded in parallel.
evidence: Directly stated with specific numerical data including standard deviation.

claim: All recorded single units were modulated by the epochs of the task or the grasp types.
source: All recorded single units were modulated by the epochs of the task or the grasp types, clearly indicating the behavioral relevance of the performed task to the detected single units (Figure 1C).
evidence: Stated in text and supported by Figure 1C showing example unit activity.

claim: Firing rates of individual units were relatively stable for different behavioral states of the task following an approximate log-normal distribution.
source: Nevertheless, in agreement with previous findings (Buzsáki and Mizuseki, 2014), firing rates of individual units were relatively stable for different behavioral states of the task following an approximate log-normal distribution (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Stated in text with citation support and reference to supplementary figure showing the distribution.

claim: The functional single neuron network of three fronto-parietal areas during active behavior is highly complex.
source: Here, we show that the functional single neuron network of three fronto-parietal areas during active behavior of macaque monkeys is highly complex.
evidence: Directly stated in the abstract as a main finding.

claim: The network was closely connected (small-world).
source: The network was closely connected (small-world) and consisted of functional modules spanning these areas.
evidence: Directly stated in the abstract as a main finding.

claim: The network consisted of functional modules spanning multiple areas.
source: The network was closely connected (small-world) and consisted of functional modules spanning these areas.
evidence: Directly stated in the abstract as a main finding.

claim: The importance of different neurons to the network was highly heterogeneous with a small number of neurons contributing strongly to the network function (hubs).
source: Surprisingly, the importance of different neurons to the network was highly heterogeneous with a small number of neurons contributing strongly to the network function (hubs), which were in turn strongly inter-connected (rich-club).
evidence: Directly stated in the abstract as a main finding.

claim: Hub neurons were strongly inter-connected forming a rich-club.
source: Surprisingly, the importance of different neurons to the network was highly heterogeneous with a small number of neurons contributing strongly to the network function (hubs), which were in turn strongly inter-connected (rich-club).
evidence: Directly stated in the abstract as a main finding.

claim: The identified rich-club consisted of neurons that were synchronized in the beta or low frequency range.
source: Examination of the network synchronization revealed that the identified rich-club consisted of neurons that were synchronized in the beta or low frequency range, whereas other neurons were mostly non-oscillatory synchronized.
evidence: Directly stated in the abstract as a main finding.

claim: Neurons outside the rich-club were mostly non-oscillatory synchronized.
source: Examination of the network synchronization revealed that the identified rich-club consisted of neurons that were synchronized in the beta or low frequency range, whereas other neurons were mostly non-oscillatory synchronized.
evidence: Directly stated in the abstract as a main finding.

claim: Oscillatory synchrony may be a central communication mechanism for highly organized functional spiking networks.
source: Therefore, oscillatory synchrony may be a central communication mechanism for highly organized functional spiking networks.
evidence: Stated as a conclusion in the abstract based on the findings.

claim: Graph theoretical approaches have enabled analysis of the brain's network topology.
source: Graph theoretical approaches have enabled analysis of the brain's network topology (Watts and Strogatz, 1998; Bullmore and Sporns, 2009).
evidence: Stated with citation support from established literature.

claim: Small-world topology is robust and allows efficient information processing.
source: Still, every region can be reached by bypassing a few others (small-world), a topology which is robust and allows efficient information processing (Hilgetag et al., 2000; Stephan et al., 2000; Bullmore and Sporns, 2009).
evidence: Stated with citation support from established literature.

claim: A few regions of the brain are highly connected and centrally located within the network (hubs).
source: A few regions of the brain are highly connected and centrally located within the network (van den Heuvel and Sporns, 2013a) (hubs) as well as strongly connected to each other (van den Heuvel et al., 2012) (rich-club).
evidence: Stated with citation support from established literature.

claim: Rich-club hubs are strongly connected to each other and form a global communication pathway across the network.
source: A few regions of the brain are highly connected and centrally located within the network (van den Heuvel and Sporns, 2013a) (hubs) as well as strongly connected to each other (van den Heuvel et al., 2012) (rich-club). This rich-club forms a global communication pathway across the network, thereby cross-linking segregated modules (van den Heuvel and Sporns, 2013b).
evidence: Stated with citation support from established literature.

claim: Neuronal modules, hubs, and rich-club organization have been shown in organotypic slices of rats.
source: While neuronal modules, hubs, and rich-club organization have been shown in organotypic slices of rats (Bonifazi et al., 2009; Shimono and Beggs, 2014; Schroeter et al., 2015), hardly anything is known about single neuron network topology in the intact brain during behavior.
evidence: Stated with citation support from previous studies.

claim: Hardly anything is known about single neuron network topology in the intact brain during behavior.
source: While neuronal modules, hubs, and rich-club organization have been shown in organotypic slices of rats (Bonifazi et al., 2009; Shimono and Beggs, 2014; Schroeter et al., 2015), hardly anything is known about single neuron network topology in the intact brain during behavior.
evidence: Stated as a knowledge gap in the field.

claim: Small-world topology has been debated in single neuron networks.
source: Only small-world topology has been debated (Yu et al., 2008; Gerhard et al., 2011) and rich-club topology has been shown recently in mice (Nigam et al., 2016).
evidence: Stated with citation support indicating ongoing debate in the literature.

claim: Rich-club topology has been shown recently in mice.
source: Only small-world topology has been debated (Yu et al., 2008; Gerhard et al., 2011) and rich-club topology has been shown recently in mice (Nigam et al., 2016).
evidence: Stated with citation support from recent literature.

claim: Oscillatory synchrony in time is a crucial feature of functional coordination.
source: Previous research has revealed oscillatory synchrony in time as a crucial feature of functional coordination (Fries, 2009; Buzsáki and Wang, 2012; Womelsdorf et al., 2014).
evidence: Stated with citation support from established literature.

claim: Gamma (40–100 Hz) and theta (4–8 Hz) frequencies are used for coordinated attention selection in visual areas and frontal cortex.
source: Different distinct frequency bands for information transmission and functional network coordination have been identified, such as gamma (40–100 Hz) and theta (4–8 Hz) in the visual areas and up to frontal cortex for coordinated attention selection (Roelfsema et al., 1997; Bosman et al., 2012; Gregoriou et al., 2012), and beta (18–35 Hz) and delta (1–4 Hz) in fronto-parietal regions for network coordination during decision and working memory processes (Brovelli et al., 2004; Pesaran et al., 2008; Haegens et al., 2011; Salazar et al., 2012; Nácher et al., 2013).
evidence: Stated with citation support from established literature.

claim: Beta (18–35 Hz) and delta (1–4 Hz) frequencies are used in fronto-parietal regions for network coordination during decision and working memory processes.
source: Different distinct frequency bands for information transmission and functional network coordination have been identified, such as gamma (40–100 Hz) and theta (4–8 Hz) in the visual areas and up to frontal cortex for coordinated attention selection (Roelfsema et al., 1997; Bosman et al., 2012; Gregoriou et al., 2012), and beta (18–35 Hz) and delta (1–4 Hz) in fronto-parietal regions for network coordination during decision and working memory processes (Brovelli et al., 2004; Pesaran et al., 2008; Haegens et al., 2011; Salazar et al., 2012; Nácher et al., 2013).
evidence: Stated with citation support from established literature.

claim: Gamma and theta oscillations have been proposed as feedforward communication frequencies across large parts of the visual network.
source: Recently, gamma and theta oscillations have been proposed as feedforward communication frequencies across large parts of the visual network, while beta oscillations have been proposed for feedback communication (Bastos et al., 2015).
evidence: Stated with citation support from recent literature.

claim: Beta oscillations have been proposed for feedback communication.
source: Recently, gamma and theta oscillations have been proposed as feedforward communication frequencies across large parts of the visual network, while beta oscillations have been proposed for feedback communication (Bastos et al., 2015).
evidence: Stated with citation support from recent literature.

claim: Firing rate correlations independent of oscillatory synchronization are important for communication in the behaving brain.
source: However, firing rate correlations have also been found, independent of oscillatory synchronization, to be of importance for communication in the behaving brain (Fujisawa et al., 2008; Smith and Kohn, 2008).
evidence: Stated with citation support from established literature.

claim: How functional network topology relates to oscillatory and non-oscillatory synchronization remains unclear.
source: Yet, how functional network topology, described by graph theoretical approaches, relates to oscillatory and non-oscillatory synchronization remains unclear.
evidence: Stated as a knowledge gap that the study aims to address.

claim: Across the three cortical areas, modular, small-world topology with a clear presence of hubs organized as a rich-club was found.
source: Across the three cortical areas we found modular, small-world topology with a clear presence of hubs that were organized as a rich-club.
evidence: Stated as a main finding in the introduction.

claim: Rich-club hub neurons predominantly spiked and communicated by oscillatory synchrony in the beta and low frequency range.
source: Moreover, rich-club hub neurons predominantly spiked and communicated by oscillatory synchrony in the beta and low frequency range, while the remainder of the network predominately communicated by non-oscillatory synchrony, suggesting that oscillatory synchrony is a central coordination mechanism for functional network topology.
evidence: Stated as a main finding in the introduction.

claim: The remainder of the network (non-hub neurons) predominantly communicated by non-oscillatory synchrony.
source: Moreover, rich-club hub neurons predominantly spiked and communicated by oscillatory synchrony in the beta and low frequency range, while the remainder of the network predominately communicated by non-oscillatory synchrony, suggesting that oscillatory synchrony is a central coordination mechanism for functional network topology.
evidence: Stated as a main finding in the introduction.

claim: Monkeys performed a visually-cued delayed grasping task with one of two different grasp types.
source: To engage the grasping motor network, monkeys performed a visually-cued delayed grasping task in which the monkey grasped a handle with one of two different grasp types (Michaels et al., 2015) (Figure 1A,B; see Materials and methods).
evidence: Directly stated in text with citation and reference to figure showing the task.

claim: Connection density was not significantly different within all distance-dependent subgroups.
source: Connection density was not significantly different within all subgroups (Kruskal-Wallis test, p>0.05).
evidence: Stated with statistical test results.

claim: Significant modular topology was present in most of the networks (Mean Q: 0.405, SD: 0.087; permutation test, p<0.05, sig. 10/12 datasets).
source: We found significant modular topology present in most of the networks (Mean Q: 0.405, SD: 0.087; permutation test, p<0.05, sig. 10/12 datasets), taking the distance-dependent decay of connectivity into account.
evidence: Stated with specific statistical results including mean, standard deviation, and significance testing.

claim: Modules were significantly predominated by units from a single area (mean largest proportion: 81.4%, SD: 14%; permutation test, p<0.001).
source: Modules were significantly predominated by units from a single area (mean largest proportion: 81.4%, SD: 14%; permutation test, p<0.001), but 84% of all modules also included units from other areas, as became apparent when visualized as anatomical networks (Figure 3D, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) or when displayed as a web where the locations of all units are determined by visualization of similarities (VOS) (Van Eck and Waltman, 2007) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: Stated with specific statistical results and reference to figures showing the modular structure.

claim: 84% of all modules also included units from other areas.
source: Modules were significantly predominated by units from a single area (mean largest proportion: 81.4%, SD: 14%; permutation test, p<0.001), but 84% of all modules also included units from other areas, as became apparent when visualized as anatomical networks (Figure 3D, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) or when displayed as a web where the locations of all units are determined by visualization of similarities (VOS) (Van Eck and Waltman, 2007) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: Stated with specific percentage and reference to figures.

claim: Significantly higher average cluster coefficients C were found in comparison to surrogate networks (mean: 0.266, SD: 0.068; permutation test, p<0.001, sig. 12/12 datasets).
source: We found significantly higher average cluster coefficients C in comparison to surrogate networks (mean: 0.266, SD: 0.068; permutation test, p<0.001, sig. 12/12 datasets) and on average similar path lengths L (mean: 3.451, SD: 0.823; mean difference to surrogate networks: −0.007; permutation test, p<0.05, sig. higher 5/12, sig. smaller 5/12 datasets).
evidence: Stated with specific statistical results including mean, standard deviation, and significance testing.

claim: Average path lengths L were on average similar to surrogate networks (mean: 3.451, SD: 0.823; mean difference to surrogate networks: −0.007).
source: We found significantly higher average cluster coefficients C in comparison to surrogate networks (mean: 0.266, SD: 0.068; permutation test, p<0.001, sig. 12/12 datasets) and on average similar path lengths L (mean: 3.451, SD: 0.823; mean difference to surrogate networks: −0.007; permutation test, p<0.05, sig. higher 5/12, sig. smaller 5/12 datasets).
evidence: Stated with specific statistical results including mean, standard deviation, and significance testing.

claim: All networks had a significant SW-coefficient (mean: 3.05, SD: 0.66; permutation test, p<0.001, sig. 12/12 datasets).
source: Consequently, all networks had a significant SW-coefficient (mean: 3.05, SD: 0.66; permutation test, p<0.001, sig. 12/12 datasets), suggesting that despite a modular structure the neuronal network is efficiently processing and transmitting information (Watts and Strogatz, 1998).
evidence: Stated with specific statistical results including mean, standard deviation, and significance testing.

claim: On average 6.27% (SD: 2.29%) of all possible connections were realized.
source: On average 6.27% (SD: 2.29%) of all possible connections were realized.
evidence: Stated with specific percentage and standard deviation.

claim: The degree distribution was heavy-tailed and best described by an exponential truncated power law model (γ = 0.6839; cutoff degree of kc = 8.657; EXPTPL: adjusted R2 = 0.9891).
source: The degree distribution (Figure 4A) was heavy-tailed and best described by an exponential truncated power law model (P(k)~kγ−1ek/kc, γ = 0.6839; cutoff degree of kc = 8.657; EXPTPL: adjusted R2 = 0.9891, including a penalty for number of fitted variables), compared to a power law (P(k)~k−γ; PL: adjusted R2 = 0.9177), exponential (EXP: adjusted R2 = 0.9742), or Gaussian (GAUS: adjusted R2 = 0.6826) model.
evidence: Stated with specific model parameters and goodness of fit measures, with reference to figure.

claim: Surrogate networks with the same distance-dependent connectivity were not heavy-tailed and were best described by a Gaussian model (GAUS: adjusted R2 = 0.9655).
source: In contrast, surrogate networks with the same distance-dependent connectivity were not heavy-tailed and were best described by a GAUS model (GAUS: adjusted R2 = 0.9655; PL: adjusted R2 = 0.3061; EXPTPL: adjusted R2 = 0.5006; EXP: adjusted R2 = 0.6419).
evidence: Stated with specific model parameters and goodness of fit measures.

claim: Networks had significantly more single units within the low, less within the intermediate, and especially more in the high degree range, than surrogate networks (cluster-based permutation test, p<0.05).
source: In agreement with the EXPTPL model, networks had significantly more single units within the low, less within the intermediate, and especially more in the high degree range, than surrogate networks (cluster-based permutation test, p<0.05), clear evidence of hubs, independent of distance-dependent connectivity.
evidence: Stated with specific statistical test results.

claim: The betweenness centrality distribution was heavy-tailed and best described by a power law model with an estimated exponent of γ = 2.212 (PL: adjusted R2 = 0.9753).
source: Similar to degree centrality, the betweenness centrality distribution (Figure 4B) was heavy-tailed and best described by a PL model, with an estimated exponent of γ = 2.212 (PL: adjusted R2 = 0.9753; EXPTPL: adjusted R2 = 0.9745; EXP: adjusted R2 = 0.9593; GAUS: adjusted R2 = −0.1509).
evidence: Stated with specific model parameters and goodness of fit measures, with reference to figure.

claim: Networks showed a significantly higher number of single units in the low and fewer units in the intermediate betweenness range than surrogate networks (cluster-based permutation test, p<0.05).
source: Statistically networks showed a significantly higher number of single units in the low and fewer units in the intermediate betweenness range than surrogate networks (cluster-based permutation test, p<0.05).
evidence: Stated with specific statistical test results.

claim: Units with high degree centrality also tended to have high betweenness centrality (r = 0.75, p<0.001, Spearman correlation).
source: Units with high degree centrality also tended to have high betweenness centrality (r = 0.75, p<0.001, Spearman correlation), suggesting a coherent group of hub units.
evidence: Stated with specific correlation coefficient and statistical significance.

claim: No significant differences in number of hubs per area were found (normalized k ≥ 9, g ≥ 0.03; Tukey's honest significant difference test on average group ranks, p<0.05).
source: We found no significant differences in number of hubs per area (normalized k ≥ 9, g ≥ 0.03; Tukey's honest significant difference test on average group ranks, p<0.05), indicating a distributed hub topology with no area acting as a network center.
evidence: Stated with specific statistical test results and hub definition criteria.

claim: Hub units showed a significantly higher level of interconnectivity than surrogate networks, with up to 15% more connections (cluster-based permutation test, p<0.05).
source: Hub units showed a significantly higher level of interconnectivity than surrogate networks, with up to 15% more connections (Figure 4D; cluster-based permutation test, p<0.05).
evidence: Stated with specific percentage and statistical test results, with reference to figure.

claim: The rich-club contained neurons from all areas with a rich-club level set to k ≥ 9% (mean rich-club neurons: 27%, SD: 18%).
source: The rich-club contained neurons from all areas with a rich-club level set to k ≥ 9% (Figure 4E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and 2C; mean rich-club neurons: 27%, SD: 18%; similar results with k set to other levels).
evidence: Stated with specific percentage, mean, and standard deviation, with reference to figures.

claim: Beta (18–35 Hz) and low frequency (3–7 Hz) oscillations were predominantly present in the spiking patterns of all datasets.
source: We found beta (18–35 Hz) and low frequency (3–7 Hz) oscillations predominantly present in the spiking patterns of all datasets (Figure 5A, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C–E).
evidence: Stated with specific frequency ranges and reference to figures showing the oscillations.

claim: Oscillatory synchrony in both frequency ranges was present more often in CCHs (mean beta: 38.3%, low: 44.3%) than in ACHs (mean beta: 22.5%, low: 31.7%).
source: Oscillatory synchrony in both frequency ranges was present more often in CCHs (mean beta: 38.3%, low: 44.3%) than in ACHs (mean beta: 22.5%, low: 31.7%), suggesting that the group of oscillating single units (oscillators; Table 2) communicates in their underlying frequency to a larger group of units.
evidence: Stated with specific percentages for both CCHs and ACHs.

claim: The degrees of all three oscillator groups were significantly higher than for non-oscillators (Tukey-Kramer test for rank, p<0.001).
source: The degrees of all three oscillator groups were significantly higher than for non-oscillators (Tukey-Kramer test for rank, p<0.001).
evidence: Stated with specific statistical test results.

claim: Betweenness centrality was significantly higher for oscillators than for non-oscillators (Tukey-Kramer test for rank, p<0.001).
source: Betweenness centrality was also significantly higher for oscillators than for non-oscillators, similar to degree centrality (Figure 5D; Tukey-Kramer test for rank, p<0.001).
evidence: Stated with specific statistical test results and reference to figure.

claim: The number of units oscillating in both frequencies was not higher than expected by coincidental overlap of the two frequency bands (permutation test, p>0.05).
source: The number of units oscillating in both frequencies was not higher than expected by coincidental overlap of the two frequency bands (permutation test, p>0.05).
evidence: Stated with specific statistical test results.

claim: The rich-club of all networks overlapped significantly with oscillating single units (permutation test, p<0.05).
source: Consequently, the rich-club of all networks overlapped significantly with oscillating single units (permutation test, p<0.05), highlighting oscillators as the backbone (van den Heuvel et al., 2012) of single unit functional connectivity (Figure 5E).
evidence: Stated with specific statistical test results and reference to figure.

claim: The number of oscillators did not differ between areas (Tukey-Kramer test for rank, p<0.05).
source: The number of oscillators did not differ between areas (Tukey-Kramer test for rank, p<0.05), in agreement with the distribution of hubs as well as rich-club units across areas.
evidence: Stated with specific statistical test results.

claim: AIP and M1 had significantly more beta oscillators than F5 (Tukey-Kramer test for rank, p<0.05).
source: Closer examination of oscillator types revealed significantly more beta oscillators in AIP and M1 than in F5, and more low frequency oscillators in F5 than in M1 and AIP (Figure 5F; Tukey-Kramer test for rank, p<0.05), reinforcing the notion that different cortical areas operate more strongly in some frequency ranges than others (Brovelli et al., 2004).
evidence: Stated with specific statistical test results and reference to figure.

claim: F5 had significantly more low frequency oscillators than M1 and AIP (Tukey-Kramer test for rank, p<0.05).
source: Closer examination of oscillator types revealed significantly more beta oscillators in AIP and M1 than in F5, and more low frequency oscillators in F5 than in M1 and AIP (Figure 5F; Tukey-Kramer test for rank, p<0.05), reinforcing the notion that different cortical areas operate more strongly in some frequency ranges than others (Brovelli et al., 2004).
evidence: Stated with specific statistical test results and reference to figure.

claim: 99% of predicted firing rate curves were positively correlated with the real firing rates of the corresponding target units.
source: Ninety-nine percent of predicted firing rate curves were positively correlated with the real firing rates of the corresponding target units (Figure 6C).
evidence: Stated with specific percentage and reference to figure.

claim: 45% of the firing rate patterns of single units could be significantly predicted by their inputs.
source: Remarkably, 45% of the firing rate patterns of our single units could be significantly predicted by their inputs.
evidence: Stated with specific percentage.

claim: The differences between grasp types and decision conditions could be significantly predicted in 9% of all cases (positive correlation: 79%).
source: The differences between grasp types and decision conditions could be significantly predicted in 9% of all cases (Figure 6D; positive correlation: 79%; shuffling of the transfer kernels and input units, p<0.05), even using this simple approach that involved no parameter fitting.
evidence: Stated with specific percentages and statistical test results, with reference to figure.

claim: The single unit network topology is highly similar to the regional network of the brain measured by EEG, MEG, DTI or fMRI.
source: The single unit network topology was highly similar to the regional network of the brain measured by EEG, MEG, DTI or fMRI (Bullmore and Sporns, 2009; Rubinov and Sporns, 2010; van den Heuvel et al., 2012; van den Heuvel and Sporns, 2013a), which strongly suggests that the observed topological properties are scale-invariant (Bullmore and Sporns, 2009).
evidence: Stated with citation support from established literature.

claim: The observed topological properties are scale-invariant.
source: The single unit network topology was highly similar to the regional network of the brain measured by EEG, MEG, DTI or fMRI (Bullmore and Sporns, 2009; Rubinov and Sporns, 2010; van den Heuvel et al., 2012; van den Heuvel and Sporns, 2013a), which strongly suggests that the observed topological properties are scale-invariant (Bullmore and Sporns, 2009).
evidence: Stated as an inference based on similarity to regional networks, with citation support.

claim: Oscillatory synchrony may act as a global coordination mechanism across the whole cortex.
source: Oscillatory synchrony may therefore act as a global coordination mechanism across the whole cortex.
evidence: Stated as an inference based on the scale-invariant properties.

claim: Oscillatory synchrony is a central element of functional network topology because it enables feed-forward coincidence detection.
source: Why is oscillatory synchrony such a central element of functional network topology? More and more evidence supports the hypothesis that information is propagated not only as a simple rate code, but by feed-forward coincidence detection accomplished by oscillatory synchrony (Fries, 2009), meaning that phase-synchronization of neurons with one another is used as a selection mechanism for information transmission.
evidence: Stated as an explanation with citation support.

claim: The advantage of oscillatory synchrony is a reduction of energy cost and rhythmic gain modulation.
source: The advantage of this mechanism is not only a reduction of energy cost, but also rhythmic gain modulation.
evidence: Stated as an explanation of the advantages of oscillatory synchrony.

claim: Synchronization over larger distances (>2 mm) is almost always oscillatory, whereas synchronization over short distances occurs also in the absence of oscillations.
source: This hypothesis is also in accordance with the finding that synchronization over larger distances (>2 mm) is almost always oscillatory, whereas synchronization over short distances occurs also in the absence of oscillations (König et al., 1995).
evidence: Stated with citation support from established literature.

claim: Beta seems to be a stabilizing signal related to the maintenance of the current sensorimotor or cognitive state.
source: Parietal and motor areas have been found to communicate via ~20 Hz beta synchronization (Pesaran et al., 2002; Brovelli et al., 2004; Pesaran et al., 2008; Dean et al., 2012) and an increment in beta band activity seems related to the maintenance of the current sensorimotor or cognitive state, in agreement with findings in the basal ganglia (Engel and Fries, 2010).
evidence: Stated with citation support from established literature.

claim: Low frequency oscillatory synchrony (1–4 Hz) is important for communication within and between the prefrontal and motor areas.
source: Oscillatory synchrony in the low frequency range (1–4 Hz) has been shown to be important for communication within and between the prefrontal and motor areas (Siegel et al., 2009; Nácher et al., 2013) and as a potential population mechanism of movement generation in motor and premotor cortex during reach initiation (Churchland et al., 2012).
evidence: Stated with citation support from established literature.

claim: A possible function of the rich-club is coordinating movement generation and initiation.
source: One possibility is that a function of the rich-club, composed of beta and low frequency oscillators spanning parietal and prefrontal cortex, is coordinating movement generation and initiation.
evidence: Stated as a speculative possibility based on the findings.

claim: Cross-frequency phase-amplitude coupling could serve as a neuronal syntax for information transmission.
source: Another possible explanation is that the power of fast oscillations is modulated by the phase of slow oscillations, termed cross-frequency phase-amplitude coupling, which could serve as a neuronal syntax for information transmission (Buzsáki, 2010; Buzsáki and Mizuseki, 2014).
evidence: Stated as a speculative possibility with citation support.

claim: The parietal lobe might be a center of beta generation.
source: This is in line with the previous findings that information via beta band is primarily transmitted from the parietal to the frontal regions and not vice versa (Brovelli et al., 2004). In areas that are hierarchically lower than the parietal lobe, such as the visual system, beta was identified as a top-down communication frequency (Bastos et al., 2015). Therefore, the parietal lobe might be a center of beta generation.
evidence: Stated as a speculative inference based on findings and citations.

claim: The center of low frequency oscillation could be in the prefrontal cortex.
source: Low frequency oscillatory synchrony during active behavior has been found predominantly in prefrontal areas (Siegel et al., 2009; Nácher et al., 2013). We speculate that the center of low frequency oscillation could be in the prefrontal cortex, suggesting that different anatomical regions generate and communicate with different frequencies.
evidence: Stated as speculation with citation support.

claim: A significant amount of the firing rate of single units could be predicted using only their network inputs.
source: We demonstrated that a significant amount of the firing rate of single units could be predicted using only their network inputs, even for complex tuning patterns, suggesting that even a small fraction of the network is enough to characterize a reasonable amount of the spatio-temporal spiking dynamics.
evidence: Stated as a finding supporting the validity of the network representation.

claim: Subsampling from a huge network with the same distance-dependent connectivity density as detected in the data did not affect the shape of the degree distribution.
source: Furthermore, we demonstrated on a model that subsampling from a huge network with the same distance-dependent connectivity density as detected in our data did not affect the shape of the degree distribution (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Stated as a finding from modeling with reference to figure.

claim: The method to detect functional connectivity corrects for common drive due to stimulus- and movement-locked inputs as well as for trial-wise fluctuations in spiking.
source: Our method to detect functional connectivity corrects for common drive due to stimulus- and movement-locked inputs as well as for trial-wise fluctuations in spiking.
evidence: Stated as a methodological feature of the analysis.

claim: Common drive pairs of simulated simple or complex networks were detected as being significant in only around 1% of all cases.
source: We investigated this possibility using our equal rate model, which included physiologically plausible firing rates and pairwise correlations. Common drive pairs of simulated simple or complex networks were detected as being significant in only around 1% of all cases, suggesting that, irrespective of the underlying topology, our method for detecting functional connectivity is hardly biased by pairwise common drive.
evidence: Stated as a finding from modeling to validate the method.

claim: 43% of all neurons on the same electrode were not connected.
source: However, we found 43% of all neurons on the same electrode to be not connected, and only sparse connectivity was found in the same area with strongly connected pairs of neurons next to unconnected pairs (e.g., Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, 2).
evidence: Stated with specific percentage and reference to figures.

claim: These results provide the first evidence of oscillatory synchrony as a central coordinating mechanism for the formation of functional network topology at the single neuron level.
source: To our knowledge, these results provide the first evidence of oscillatory synchrony as a central coordinating mechanism for the formation of functional network topology at the single neuron level.
evidence: Stated as a main conclusion of the study.

claim: Oscillating neurons form a backbone for functional connectivity spanning several areas.
source: By demonstrating that oscillating neurons form a backbone for functional connectivity, spanning several areas, we provide a unified basis for understanding the neuronal computations coordinating and generating behavior at the network level.
evidence: Stated as a main conclusion of the study.

claim: Neural activity was recorded simultaneously from many channels in two female and one male rhesus macaque monkey.
source: Neural activity was recorded simultaneously from many channels in two female and one male rhesus macaque monkey (Animals S, Z, and M; body weight 9, 7, and 10 kg, respectively).
evidence: Directly stated in the methods section.

claim: All procedures and animal care were in accordance with German and European law.
source: All procedures and animal care were in accordance with German and European law and were in agreement with the Guidelines for the Care and Use of Mammals in Neuroscience and Behavioral Research (National Research Council, 2003).
evidence: Stated as compliance with ethical guidelines with citation.

claim: Each animal was implanted with two floating microelectrode arrays per area (FMAs; 32 electrodes; spacing between electrodes: 400 μm).
source: In short, each animal was implanted with two floating microelectrode arrays per area (FMAs; Microprobes for Life Sciences; 32 electrodes; spacing between electrodes: 400 μm; length: 1.5 to 7.1 mm monotonically increasing to target grey matter along the sulcus).
evidence: Directly stated in the methods section with specific technical details.

claim: Animal M was implanted with a total of six FMAs in areas AIP, F5, and M1 in the left hemisphere.
source: Animal M was implanted with a total of six FMAs in the same cortical areas and two additional arrays in area M1, in the left hemisphere (Figure 1B).
evidence: Directly stated in the methods section with reference to figure.

claim: Directed functional connections could be detected with 62% hits for simple networks and 69% hits for complex networks.
source: We could detect directed functional connections reasonably well (hits: 62% for SN, and 69% for CN) and hardly detected any false connections (correct rejections (CR) > 99% for SN and CN), independent of the underlying topology (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: Stated with specific percentages from modeling validation with reference to figure.

claim: The average bidirectional CCH had a 24 times higher peak than the average common drive CCH.
source: In direct comparison, the average common drive CCH as well as the average bidirectional CCH had a maximum at the zero time lag, but with the average bidirectional CCH having a 24 times higher peak (10.89 SD surrogate for bidirectional connections, and 0.45 SD surrogate for common drive; Figure 2—figure supplement 3E), which is well in line with around 1% of all common drive pairs were detected as significant.
evidence: Stated with specific numerical comparison from modeling with reference to figure.

claim: More than 7 times more bidirectional connections had a peak at the 0 time lag than common drive pairs.
source: When analyzing the distribution of maximum peaks in more detail, we found more than 7 times more bidirectional connections having a peak at the 0 time lag than common drive pairs (Figure 2—figure supplement 3F), in line with the results from the models described above (Vicente et al., 2008; Gollo et al., 2014).
evidence: Stated with specific numerical comparison from modeling with reference to figure and citations.

claim: 45.67% of maximum peaks or troughs had a time lag less than 10 ms, and 85.12% had a time lag less than 100 ms.
source: Interestingly, the maximum peak or trough time lag distribution showed an exponential decay, with most of the peaks or troughs having a very short time lag (45.67% < 10 ms, and 85.12% < 100 ms), indicating predominantly direct influences of the units on each other.
evidence: Stated with specific percentages from data analysis.

claim: For beta connections, 77.70% of phase lags were within half a cycle around the zero time lag.
source: The majority of phase lags were within half a cycle around the zero time lag for both frequencies (beta connections: 77.70% < π, low frequency connections: 87.66% < π), suggesting that for most oscillatory synchronized connections we could accurately determine which unit was leading and which unit was lagging.
evidence: Stated with specific percentages from data analysis.

claim: For low frequency connections, 87.66% of phase lags were within half a cycle around the zero time lag.
source: The majority of phase lags were within half a cycle around the zero time lag for both frequencies (beta connections: 77.70% < π, low frequency connections: 87.66% < π), suggesting that for most oscillatory synchronized connections we could accurately determine which unit was leading and which unit was lagging.
evidence: Stated with specific percentages from data analysis.

claim: An average of 17.75 units (SD: 9.56) were dropped from analysis as they were not connected to the largest inter-connected component.
source: For analyzing the functional network topology, all units not connected to the largest inter-connected component were first discarded (mean number of units dropped: 17.75, SD: 9.56; mean percentage: 23.5%, SD: 13.3%; Table 1) and binary directional connectivity matrices were created for every dataset (Figure 3A).
evidence: Stated with specific mean and standard deviation.

claim: The high oscillatory state network showed a clear rich-club topology, whereas the low oscillatory state network hardly showed any rich-club effect.
source: However, when comparing the rich-club level there was a striking difference for higher rich-club levels (Figure 5—figure supplement 3D). In both datasets, the high oscillatory state network showed a clear rich-club topology, whereas the low oscillatory state network hardly showed any rich-club effect.
evidence: Stated as a finding from analysis of oscillatory state-dependent networks with reference to figure.

claim: A rich-club topology is only present when there is a high level of oscillatory synchrony in the network.
source: These results suggest that a rich-cub topology is only present when there is a high level of oscillatory synchrony in the network.
evidence: Stated as an inference from the oscillatory state analysis.
